name: Kubo transport coefficients of the QGP
summary: QGP shear and bulk viscosities, conductivity and heavy-quark diffusion are defined by Kubo formulas. Lattice QCD obtains them from Euclidean correlators by inverting to spectral functions, an ill-posed analytic continuation, and flow data give η/s≈1–2 × ħ/4πk_B, near the holographic value.
sources: Kovtun, Son & Starinets (2005). "Viscosity in Strongly Interacting Quantum Field Theories from Black Hole Physics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 111601. [arXiv:hep-th/0405231](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0405231)

name: Giant resonances as nuclear linear response
summary: Giant dipole and monopole resonances are the nucleus's linear response to an external field. RPA is the time-dependent mean-field susceptibility, and energy-weighted sum rules (Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn) are f-sum rules fixed by commutators, as for conductivity or dielectric response.

name: Fano factor: sub-Poisson ionization statistics
summary: The number of ion pairs or electron–hole pairs created by a stopped particle fluctuates less than Poisson (Fano factor F≈0.1 in Ge), because total energy is fixed, as with microcanonical fluctuations. F sets the intrinsic energy resolution of gas and semiconductor detectors.
sources: Fano (1947). "Ionization Yield of Radiations. II. The Fluctuations of the Number of Ions". *Phys. Rev.* 72, 26. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.72.26](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.72.26)

name: Jet transverse-momentum broadening as diffusion
summary: A fast parton crossing the plasma takes random transverse kicks, so its transverse momentum random-walks: ⟨k_⊥²⟩=q̂L, with q̂ a momentum-diffusion coefficient. The coherent sum of induced radiation over this random walk gives the BDMPS ΔE∝q̂L² energy loss.
map: \langle k_\perp^2\rangle=\hat qL,\ \hat q=\rho\int d^2q_\perp q_\perp^2\frac{d\sigma}{d^2q_\perp};\ \Delta E\propto\alpha_s\hat qL^2
sources: Baier et al. (1997). "Radiative energy loss of high energy quarks and gluons in a finite-volume quark-gluon plasma". *Nucl. Phys. B* 483, 291. [arXiv:hep-ph/9607355](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9607355)

name: Heavy quarks as Brownian particles in the QGP
summary: Charm and bottom quarks (M≫T) diffuse through the plasma like Brownian particles. A Langevin equation with drag η_D and momentum-diffusion κ obeys the Einstein relation η_D=κ/2MT, and the spatial diffusion coefficient 2πTD_s is extracted from heavy-flavour R_AA and v₂.
sources: Moore & Teaney (2005). "How much do heavy quarks thermalize in a heavy ion collision?". *Phys. Rev. C* 71, 064904. [arXiv:hep-ph/0412346](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0412346)

name: Kramers escape theory was built for nuclear fission
summary: Kramers' 1940 theory of thermally activated escape over a barrier was motivated by Bohr–Wheeler fission and treated the fissioning nucleus as a Brownian particle in a viscous medium. Nuclear dissipation still appears as the Kramers factor that reduces fission rates and enhances pre-scission neutron emission.
sources: Kramers (1940). "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)
Bohr & Wheeler (1939). "The Mechanism of Nuclear Fission". *Phys. Rev.* 56, 426. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.56.426](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.56.426)

name: Radioactive decay as a Poisson process
summary: Decay is a memoryless Markov process: counts are Poisson, waiting times exponential, and decay chains obey Bateman's linear master equations. Counting statistics and dead-time corrections in nuclear detectors use the same stochastic-process tools.

name: Shape phase transitions in finite nuclei
summary: As nucleon number changes, nuclei go from spherical vibrators to deformed rotors through quantum shape phase transitions. Their Landau-theory description uses the quadrupole deformation as order parameter, and analytic critical-point symmetries such as X(5) and E(5) describe nuclei at the transition, which finite size rounds into crossovers.
sources: Iachello (2001). "Analytic Description of Critical Point Nuclei in a Spherical-Axially Deformed Shape Phase Transition". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 87, 052502. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.052502](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.052502)

name: QCD critical point in the 3D Ising class
summary: A QCD critical endpoint, if it exists, lies in the 3D Ising (Z₂) universality class. (T, μ_B) map linearly onto Ising (t, h), and net-proton cumulant ratios scale with powers of ξ (κσ²∝ξ⁷), so beam-energy scans hunt for non-monotonic kurtosis. Finite-size scaling of cumulants is used to locate it.
sources: Stephanov (2009). "Non-Gaussian fluctuations near the QCD critical point". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 102, 032301. [arXiv:0809.3450](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.3450)
Stephanov, Rajagopal & Shuryak (1998). "Signatures of the Tricritical Point in QCD". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 81, 4816. [arXiv:hep-ph/9806219](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9806219)
Sorensen & Sorensen (2024). "Locating the QCD critical point with finite-size scaling of proton cumulants". [arXiv:2405.10278](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10278)

name: Relativistic mean-field theory of dense matter
summary: The Walecka σ–ω model replaces meson fields by their mean values, a Hartree mean-field theory in the spirit of Weiss. It reproduces nuclear saturation and gives a stiff neutron-star EOS, and Skyrme and RMF density functionals remain the main EOS inputs beyond ab initio densities.
sources: Walecka (1974). "A theory of highly condensed matter". *Ann. Phys.* 83, 491. [doi:10.1016/0003-4916(74)90208-5](https://doi.org/10.1016/0003-4916(74)90208-5)

name: BCS pairing in nuclei
summary: Odd–even mass staggering, gaps in even–even spectra and reduced moments of inertia show that nucleons pair as in a superconductor. A BCS/Bogoliubov mean field with Δ≈12/√A MeV describes it, and the gap equation is the Landau–Ginzburg/BCS mean field of 03 applied to a finite Fermi system.
sources: Bohr, Mottelson & Pines (1958). "Possible Analogy between the Excitation Spectra of Nuclei and Those of the Superconducting Metallic State". *Phys. Rev.* 110, 936. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.110.936](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.110.936)

name: DGLAP evolution as a renormalization-group equation
summary: Q² dependence of parton distributions is the RG running of twist-2 operator matrix elements. Mellin moments scale with anomalous dimensions γ_n, exactly like scaling operators near a fixed point, and Bjorken scaling is the free-field fixed point of asymptotically free QCD.
sources: Altarelli & Parisi (1977). "Asymptotic freedom in parton language". *Nucl. Phys. B* 126, 298. [doi:10.1016/0550-3213(77)90384-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213(77)90384-4)

name: SRG and V_low-k: Wilsonian RG for nuclear forces
summary: The similarity renormalization group (and IMSRG) is a continuous unitary RG flow that decouples high- and low-momentum states, the Wilsonian idea of integrating out short distances while keeping observables. It makes nuclear many-body calculations converge and generates induced three-body forces, the analogue of irrelevant couplings generated under RG.
sources: Bogner, Furnstahl & Schwenk (2010). "From low-momentum interactions to nuclear structure". *Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys.* 65, 94. [arXiv:0912.3688](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.3688)

name: Efimov physics as an RG limit cycle
summary: Renormalizing the three-boson problem with contact interactions needs a three-body force whose coupling runs periodically in ln Λ: an RG limit cycle rather than a fixed point. This produces discrete scale invariance and the Efimov ratio 22.7, seen in cold atoms, light nuclei and halo systems.
sources: Bedaque, Hammer & van Kolck (1999). "Renormalization of the Three-Body System with Short-Range Interactions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 82, 463. [arXiv:nucl-th/9809025](https://arxiv.org/abs/nucl-th/9809025)

name: Spin ice and Pauling's residual entropy
summary: On the pyrochlore lattice of Dy₂Ti₂O₇ and Ho₂Ti₂O₇, the 'two-in, two-out' rule is Pauling's ice rule for protons in water ice, so the ground state is macroscopically degenerate. Heat-capacity measurements recovered Pauling's residual entropy of $\frac R2\ln\frac32$ per mole of spins, an apparent exception to the third law that only weak residual interactions acting over very long equilibration times can lift.

name: Motility-induced phase separation as liquid–gas coexistence
summary: Self-propelled particles that slow down where crowded separate into dense and dilute phases without any attraction (motility-induced phase separation). To leading order the dynamics maps onto an effective free energy, giving a spinodal at $d\ln v/d\ln\rho<-1$ and a coexistence that resembles the liquid–gas transition.
breaks: There is no equilibrium free energy: binodals do not follow a Maxwell construction on $\mu_{\rm eff}$, and mechanical pressure need not balance in the usual way. Gradient terms can also produce reverse Ostwald ripening and microphase separation.
sources: Marchetti et al. (2013). "Hydrodynamics of soft active matter". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1143. [arXiv:1207.2929](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2929)

name: Jamming as a critical point of disordered packings
summary: Athermal packings jam at the isostatic point, where the mean contact number reaches $z_c=2d$. Above it, excess contacts and shear modulus scale as powers of $\phi-\phi_J$, as near a critical point. Liu and Nagel's jamming phase diagram links this to the glass transition, and the infinite-dimensional replica solution ties jamming to marginal stability and full replica-symmetry breaking (the Gardner phase).
sources: Liu & Nagel (1998). "Jamming is not just cool any more". *Nature* 396, 21. [doi:10.1038/23819](https://doi.org/10.1038/23819)

name: Weak localization and scaling theory in metals
summary: Constructive interference of time-reversed backscattering paths lowers the conductance of disordered metals (weak localization). A magnetic field or dephasing cuts it off, and it leaves universal conductance fluctuations of order $e^2/h$. One-parameter scaling in the dimensionless conductance $g$ predicts that all states localize in 1D and 2D (without spin–orbit coupling) and that 3D has a mobility edge.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: Altland–Zirnbauer classes become the tenfold way
summary: The ten symmetry classes of disordered Hamiltonians, built from time-reversal, particle–hole and chiral symmetry (Altland–Zirnbauer), are the same ten classes that classify gapped topological insulators and superconductors. In each dimension the classes with a nontrivial invariant are those whose boundary modes cannot be Anderson-localized, one of the routes to the periodic table (Schnyder–Ryu–Furusaki–Ludwig, Kitaev).
sources: Qi & Zhang (2011). "Topological insulators and superconductors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 83, 1057. [arXiv:1008.2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2026)

name: Quantum Hall plateau transition as Anderson localization
summary: Quantized plateaus need disorder: states in the Landau-level tails are Anderson-localized and leave $\sigma_{xy}$ unchanged, while only one energy per level is extended. The plateau-to-plateau transition is a localization–delocalization critical point with $\nu\approx2.6$ (Chalker–Coddington network), not the classical-percolation value $4/3$, and its width shrinks as $T^{\kappa}$.
sources: von Klitzing, Dorda & Pepper (1980). "New Method for High-Accuracy Determination of the Fine-Structure Constant Based on Quantized Hall Resistance". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 45, 494. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.494)
Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: Gelation is percolation
summary: Flory–Stockmayer gelation theory is percolation on a Bethe lattice, and the sol–gel transition of crosslinking polymers is a connectivity-percolation threshold, with the gel fraction as order parameter and percolation scaling for the finite clusters. Close to the gel point, 3D percolation exponents replace the Flory–Stockmayer mean-field values (de Gennes, Stauffer).
sources: Broadbent & Hammersley (1957). "Percolation processes: I. Crystals and mazes". *Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc.* 53, 629. [doi:10.1017/S0305004100032680](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100032680)

name: Dilute magnetic alloys: RKKY makes spin glasses
summary: The canonical spin glasses are dilute magnetic alloys (CuMn, AuFe) whose moments couple by RKKY exchange, which oscillates in sign with distance. Random positions therefore give random-sign couplings, the physical basis of the Edwards–Anderson model, and the susceptibility cusp at $T_f$ marks the freezing; insulating spin glasses such as Eu$_x$Sr$_{1-x}$S arise instead from competing ferro- and antiferromagnetic exchange.
map: J_{\rm RKKY}(r)\propto\frac{\cos(2k_Fr)}{(2k_Fr)^3},\quad H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j,\ J_{ij}\ \text{random}
sources: Edwards & Anderson (1975). "Theory of spin glasses". *J. Phys. F* 5, 965. [doi:10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017)

name: Frustration with and without disorder
summary: Both start from frustration: when the couplings around a loop have a negative product, no spin arrangement satisfies all of them, and many low-energy states result. With quenched random couplings the spins freeze into a spin glass with Edwards–Anderson order $q$. Geometric frustration on clean triangular, kagome or pyrochlore lattices can instead give order by disorder, spin ice or a quantum spin liquid, and a little bond disorder often turns such magnets into spin glasses.
breaks: A spin glass needs quenched randomness and freezes into a static random state governed by replica-symmetry breaking. A spin liquid is clean, can stay dynamic down to T=0 and is characterised by long-range entanglement and fractionalized excitations, which have no spin-glass counterpart.
sources: Edwards & Anderson (1975). "Theory of spin glasses". *J. Phys. F* 5, 965. [doi:10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017)
Balents (2010). "Spin liquids in frustrated magnets". *Nature* 464, 199. [doi:10.1038/nature08917](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08917)

name: Spin-glass theory of the structural glass transition
summary: Mean-field $p$-spin glasses have a dynamical transition at $T_d$, whose equations coincide with mode-coupling theory of supercooled liquids, and a Kauzmann-like entropy crisis at $T_K$; together these form the random first-order transition theory of glasses (Kirkpatrick, Thirumalai, Wolynes). Aging, rugged landscapes and replica methods carry over, culminating in the exact solution for hard spheres in infinite dimensions.
breaks: Structural glasses have no quenched disorder; it is self-generated. The sharp mean-field $T_d$ becomes a crossover in finite dimensions, and the Edwards–Anderson Ising spin glass (full RSB, continuous transition) belongs to a different class from the one-step RSB models that mimic glasses.
sources: Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)
Debenedetti & Stillinger (2001). "Supercooled liquids and the glass transition". *Nature* 410, 259. [doi:10.1038/35065704](https://doi.org/10.1038/35065704)

name: Topological entanglement entropy
summary: In a gapped 2D phase the entanglement entropy of a region obeys an area law with a universal constant correction, $S_A=\alpha L-\gamma$, where $\gamma=\ln\mathcal D$ is set by the anyons' quantum dimensions (Kitaev–Preskill, Levin–Wen). This information-theoretic quantity detects topological order without a local order parameter; $\gamma=\ln2$ for the toric code and $\mathbb Z_2$ spin liquids.

name: Bethe ansatz and spinons in Heisenberg chains
summary: Bethe's 1931 solution of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain founded the Bethe ansatz; its elementary excitations are spin-1/2 spinons, created in pairs, with the des Cloizeaux–Pearson dispersion. Neutron scattering on chain compounds such as KCuF₃ sees the predicted two-spinon continuum instead of sharp magnons.
sources: Bethe (1931). "Zur Theorie der Metalle". *Z. Phys.* 71, 205. [doi:10.1007/BF01341708](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01341708)

name: Kitaev honeycomb model and Kitaev materials
summary: Kitaev's honeycomb model, with bond-dependent Ising couplings, is solved exactly by writing the spins as Majorana fermions in a static $\mathbb Z_2$ gauge field; it has gapped and gapless spin liquids and, in a magnetic field, a non-Abelian phase. Jackeli and Khaliullin showed that edge-sharing $j=1/2$ magnets approximate it, launching the search in iridates and α-RuCl₃, whose reported half-quantized thermal Hall effect remains contested.
sources: Kitaev (2006). "Anyons in an exactly solved model and beyond". *Ann. Phys.* 321, 2. [arXiv:cond-mat/0506438](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0506438)
Balents (2010). "Spin liquids in frustrated magnets". *Nature* 464, 199. [doi:10.1038/nature08917](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08917)

name: Degenerate electrons and phonon gas in solids
summary: Conduction electrons form a degenerate Fermi gas: only a fraction $k_BT/E_F$ near the Fermi surface is excited, giving the Sommerfeld heat capacity $\gamma T$, Pauli paramagnetism and the Fermi–Dirac carrier statistics of semiconductors. Phonons are a Bose gas with zero chemical potential and give the Debye $T^3$ law, so a metal's low-temperature heat capacity is $\gamma T+\beta T^3$.

name: Excitons as composite bosons: 2D exciton condensates
summary: Interlayer excitons in transition-metal-dichalcogenide double layers are long-lived composite bosons that, at low temperature and density, should Bose-condense, which in 2D means a BKT superfluid. Experiments on TMD double layers report signatures of exciton condensation and excitonic insulators.
breaks: Excitons behave as bosons only when $n_Xa_X^2\ll1$; at higher density, exchange between their fermionic constituents and screening dissociate them into an electron–hole plasma (the excitonic Mott transition). Disorder and finite lifetime further limit coherence.

name: BCS–BEC crossover: Cooper pairs to Bose condensate
summary: Cooper's bound state exists only because the filled Fermi sea blocks the states below $k_F$. As the attraction grows, large overlapping Cooper pairs turn continuously into tightly bound bosonic molecules that Bose-condense, so $T_c$ rises from the exponentially small BCS value to about $0.218\,T_F$; this crossover was realised with Feshbach-tuned ultracold fermions.
breaks: A conventional superconductor is not a BEC of preformed pairs: the pair size far exceeds the spacing between pairs, and $T_c$ is set by pair breaking, not by the onset of phase coherence.
sources: Cooper (1956). "Bound Electron Pairs in a Degenerate Fermi Gas". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 1189. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.1189](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.1189)
Bardeen, Cooper & Schrieffer (1957). "Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 108, 1175. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175)

name: Soft matter as the laboratory of stochastic thermodynamics
summary: Because soft-matter energies are of order $k_BT$, colloids in optical traps have been used to test the fluctuation theorem, the Jarzynski and Crooks relations and Landauer's erasure bound. Colloidal and polymer glasses show aging and fluctuation–dissipation violations, which are described with an effective temperature.
map: \langle e^{-\beta W}\rangle=e^{-\beta\Delta F},\quad \langle Q_{\rm erase}\rangle\ge k_BT\ln2
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: Active particles break fluctuation–dissipation
summary: Active Brownian particles obey Langevin dynamics plus persistent self-propulsion, so long-time diffusion far exceeds the Stokes–Einstein value and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem fails. Mechanical pressure on a wall can depend on the wall potential, so pressure is not in general a state function.
breaks: No single effective temperature exists: trapped-particle distributions, equations of state and fluctuation–dissipation ratios each give a different value, and the steady state depends on dynamical details that equilibrium ignores.
sources: Marchetti et al. (2013). "Hydrodynamics of soft active matter". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1143. [arXiv:1207.2929](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2929)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Active matter as a driven non-equilibrium steady state
summary: Self-propulsion injects energy at every particle and breaks detailed balance locally, so active fluids are non-equilibrium steady states with nonzero entropy production. Active lattice gases are exclusion processes with persistent hopping, and the signatures of driven systems (currents, long-range correlations, giant number fluctuations $\Delta N\propto N^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha>1/2$) appear in flocks and active nematics.
sources: Marchetti et al. (2013). "Hydrodynamics of soft active matter". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1143. [arXiv:1207.2929](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2929)

name: Boltzmann equation for Bloch electrons
summary: The semiclassical Boltzmann equation with Bloch velocities, a Fermi–Dirac equilibrium and a relaxation time gives the Drude conductivity, Hall coefficient, thermopower and Wiedemann–Franz law; only states within $k_BT$ of the Fermi surface contribute. Where electron–electron collisions conserve momentum, as in graphene's Dirac fluid, the same kinetic theory gives electron hydrodynamics and violations of Wiedemann–Franz.
map: \partial_tf+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf r}f-\frac{e}{\hbar}(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf k}f=-\frac{f-f_0}{\tau},\ \sigma=\frac{ne^2\tau}{m^*}
breaks: It fails where quantum interference matters (weak localization) and in correlated metals without quasiparticles.

name: Kinetic theory of the phonon gas
summary: Lattice heat conduction is the kinetic theory of a phonon gas: the Peierls–Boltzmann equation gives $\kappa=\tfrac13C_Vv\ell$, the dilute-gas formula. Only Umklapp collisions relax crystal momentum, so $\kappa$ grows exponentially on cooling until boundary scattering takes over; when momentum-conserving normal processes dominate, phonons flow hydrodynamically and carry second sound.

name: Kubo formula and Johnson–Nyquist noise
summary: Electrical conductivity is a current–current correlation function (the Kubo or Green–Kubo formula), and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem fixes every resistor's equilibrium voltage noise at $S_V=4k_BTR$ (Johnson–Nyquist). The same Kubo formula, evaluated for Bloch bands, gives TKNN's quantized Hall conductance.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Neutron scattering measures the dynamic susceptibility
summary: The magnetic inelastic neutron cross-section is proportional to the dynamic structure factor $S(\mathbf q,\omega)$, which the fluctuation–dissipation theorem equates to the absorptive susceptibility $\chi''(\mathbf q,\omega)$ times a Bose factor. Magnon dispersions, critical scattering near $T_c$ and spinon continua are therefore measured response functions, and detailed balance between $\pm\omega$ serves as a built-in check.
map: S(\mathbf q,\omega)\propto\frac{\chi''(\mathbf q,\omega)}{1-e^{-\hbar\omega/k_BT}},\quad S(\mathbf q,-\omega)=e^{-\hbar\omega/k_BT}S(\mathbf q,\omega)
sources: Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Colloids as Brownian particles; grains as athermal limit
summary: Colloidal particles are the Brownian particles of Einstein's 1905 theory and Perrin's experiments: they follow overdamped Langevin dynamics with Stokes–Einstein diffusion, and an optically trapped colloid is a textbook Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Granular grains obey the same mechanics with $k_BT$ negligible against gravity, so driving must replace temperature and fluctuation–dissipation no longer holds.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 549. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053220806)

name: Rouse, Zimm and reptation: Langevin dynamics of chains
summary: A polymer modelled as beads joined by entropic springs, each bead obeying overdamped Langevin dynamics, splits into Rouse modes with longest time $\tau_R\propto N^2$; hydrodynamic interactions turn this into Zimm scaling $\tau\propto N^{3\nu}$. In entangled melts, de Gennes' reptation treats the chain as a random walker confined to a tube, giving $\tau_d\propto N^3$ (experimentally about $N^{3.4}$).
map: \zeta\dot{\mathbf R}_n=k(\mathbf R_{n+1}-2\mathbf R_n+\mathbf R_{n-1})+\mathbf f_n,\quad \tau_R\propto N^2,\ \tau_d\propto N^3
sources: de Gennes (1971). "Reptation of a Polymer Chain in the Presence of Fixed Obstacles". *J. Chem. Phys.* 55, 572. [doi:10.1063/1.1675789](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1675789)

name: RCSJ junction: Brownian particle in a tilted washboard
summary: In the resistively and capacitively shunted junction model, the phase difference $\varphi$ is a damped particle of mass $\propto C$ in the tilted washboard $U=-E_J\cos\varphi-(\hbar I/2e)\varphi$, kicked by the shunt's Johnson noise. Thermal switching out of the zero-voltage state is Kramers escape, and below $T^*\approx\hbar\omega_p/2\pi k_B$ macroscopic quantum tunnelling of $\varphi$ takes over (Caldeira–Leggett).
sources: Josephson (1962). "Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling". *Phys. Lett.* 1, 251. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0)

name: Quantum–classical mapping and Hertz–Millis theory
summary: In imaginary time a quantum transition in $d$ dimensions becomes a classical one in $d+z$ dimensions, so Landau–Ginzburg–Wilson theory, the RG and the Ginzburg criterion carry over. Hertz–Millis theory applies this to metallic magnets: Landau damping gives $z=3$ for ferromagnets and $z=2$ for antiferromagnets, and a quantum critical fan opens above $g_c$, bounded by $k_BT\sim|g-g_c|^{z\nu}$.
breaks: Hertz–Millis fails in 2D metals and at Kondo-breakdown transitions, where the fermions cannot be integrated out and local quantum criticality or non-Fermi-liquid physics appears.
sources: Sachdev & Keimer (2011). "Quantum criticality". *Physics Today* 64, 29. [arXiv:1102.4628](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.4628)

Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)

name: Self-avoiding polymers are the n→0 O(n) model
summary: De Gennes showed that self-avoiding-walk statistics are the $n\to0$ limit of the $O(n)$ spin model, with $1/N$ playing the role of reduced temperature. A polymer's size exponent is therefore a critical exponent, computable by the $\epsilon$ expansion and Monte Carlo ($\nu\approx0.588$ in 3D, exactly $3/4$ in 2D); Flory's mean-field $3/(d+2)$ is close but not exact.
sources: Flory (1949). "The Configuration of Real Polymer Chains". *J. Chem. Phys.* 17, 303. [doi:10.1063/1.1747243](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1747243)

Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)

name: Quantum critical scaling and ω/T collapse
summary: A zero-temperature transition has $\xi\sim|g-g_c|^{-\nu}$ and $\xi_\tau\sim\xi^z$. Above it temperature is the only scale, so responses collapse onto functions of $\hbar\omega/k_BT$, and universality classes carry over from classical ones (the transverse-field Ising chain has 2D Ising exponents). Heavy-fermion metals such as CeCu$_{6-x}$Au$_x$ show $\omega/T$ scaling with anomalous exponents that no known class reproduces.
sources: Sachdev & Keimer (2011). "Quantum criticality". *Physics Today* 64, 29. [arXiv:1102.4628](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.4628)
Kadanoff (1966). "Scaling laws for Ising models near Tc". *Physics* 2, 263. [doi:10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.2.263](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.2.263)

name: Mermin–Wagner, anisotropy and order in 2D magnets
summary: The Mermin–Wagner theorem forbids order at $T>0$ in isotropic 2D Heisenberg magnets. Parent cuprates such as La₂CuO₄ therefore show only exponentially growing correlations, $\xi\propto e^{2\pi\rho_s/k_BT}$, and order through weak interlayer coupling. Ising anisotropy evades the theorem, giving Onsager-class transitions in Rb₂CoF₄ and long-range order in monolayer CrI₃.
sources: Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)
Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Lattice spin models as effective magnet Hamiltonians
summary: Exchange between local moments gives the Heisenberg Hamiltonian, and crystal-field or exchange anisotropy reduces it to the Ising or XY models of statistical mechanics, so real magnets are where those models are tested. Neutron and susceptibility data on FeF₂ (3D Ising) and Rb₂CoF₄ (2D Ising), among others, confirm the predicted universality classes.
map: H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j-D\sum_i(S_i^z)^2\ \xrightarrow{D\gg J}\ -J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\sigma_i\sigma_j
breaks: Real moments are quantum: spin-1/2 fluctuations shrink the ordered moment and can destroy order. Dipolar, RKKY or longer-range couplings can also change the universality class.
sources: Ising (1925). "Beitrag zur Theorie des Ferromagnetismus". *Z. Phys.* 31, 253. [doi:10.1007/BF02980577](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02980577)
Heisenberg (1928). "Zur Theorie des Ferromagnetismus". *Z. Phys.* 49, 619. [doi:10.1007/BF01328601](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01328601)

name: Vicsek flocks: a moving XY model beating Mermin–Wagner
summary: The Vicsek model is an XY ferromagnet whose spins are velocities that also move the particles, so alignment is coupled to density by self-advection. Toner and Tu showed that this coupling allows true long-range polar order in 2D, which Mermin–Wagner forbids for the equilibrium XY model.
breaks: There is no Hamiltonian or Boltzmann weight. The flocking transition is discontinuous, proceeding through travelling bands as a phase-separation scenario, rather than an XY critical point, and setting $v_0\to0$ recovers the equilibrium XY model without long-range order.
sources: Vicsek et al. (1995). "Novel Type of Phase Transition in a System of Self-Driven Particles". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 75, 1226. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226)

Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

name: Landau–de Gennes theory of liquid crystals
summary: The nematic order parameter is a traceless symmetric tensor $Q_{ij}$, and because symmetry allows a $\mathrm{tr}\,Q^3$ term, Landau theory predicts a first-order isotropic–nematic transition (weakly first order in practice), with Maier–Saupe theory as its microscopic mean-field counterpart. De Gennes mapped the nematic–smectic-A transition, a complex density-wave order parameter coupled to director fluctuations, onto the Ginzburg–Landau theory of superconductors.
sources: de Gennes (1992). "Soft matter". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 64, 645. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.64.645](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.64.645)

name: DMFT: Weiss mean field for quantum lattices
summary: Dynamical mean-field theory replaces a site's lattice environment by a self-consistent, frequency-dependent bath, the quantum analogue of the Weiss molecular field, and is exact in infinite dimensions with hopping scaled as $t\propto1/\sqrt d$. Because it keeps all local quantum fluctuations it captures the Mott metal–insulator transition that static mean field misses, and cluster extensions restore short-range spatial correlations.
sources: Georges, Kotliar, Krauth & Rozenberg (1996). "Dynamical mean-field theory of strongly correlated fermion systems and the limit of infinite dimensions". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 68, 13. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.68.13](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.68.13)

name: BCS as mean field; Ginzburg–Landau as its Landau theory
summary: BCS theory is a self-consistent mean-field decoupling in the pair amplitude $\Delta$. Gor'kov showed that near $T_c$ it reduces to Ginzburg–Landau theory, a Landau expansion in a complex order parameter minimally coupled to $\mathbf A$. Because the Ginzburg number of clean low-$T_c$ metals scales as $(k_BT_c/E_F)^4$, the fluctuation region is too narrow to observe and mean-field exponents are effectively exact.
breaks: The order parameter is not gauge-invariant, and fluctuations of $\mathbf A$ can make the transition weakly first order (Halperin–Lubensky–Ma). In short-coherence-length superconductors a real fluctuation window opens.
sources: Bardeen, Cooper & Schrieffer (1957). "Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 108, 1175. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175)

name: Where mean field fails: phase fluctuations in cuprates
summary: Short coherence lengths (1–2 nm), low superfluid density and quasi-2D layering raise the cuprates' Ginzburg number by many orders of magnitude over BCS metals, and YBCO shows 3D-XY critical behaviour near $T_c$. In underdoped samples $T_c$ tracks the superfluid stiffness (Uemura scaling), and a Nernst signal and diamagnetism persist above $T_c$, suggesting that phase fluctuations rather than gap closing set $T_c$ (Emery–Kivelson).
sources: Keimer et al. (2015). "From quantum matter to high-temperature superconductivity in copper oxides". *Nature* 518, 179. [doi:10.1038/nature14165](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14165)
Lee, Nagaosa & Wen (2006). "Doping a Mott insulator: Physics of high-temperature superconductivity". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 78, 17. [arXiv:cond-mat/0410445](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0410445)

name: Wilson's numerical RG solves the Kondo problem
summary: The antiferromagnetic Kondo coupling is marginally relevant: Anderson's poor-man's scaling makes it grow as the bandwidth is reduced, generating the scale $T_K$. Wilson's numerical renormalization group followed this flow nonperturbatively to the screened Fermi-liquid fixed point (Wilson ratio $R_W=2$), the RG's first nonperturbative success outside critical phenomena.
sources: Wilson (1975). "The renormalization group: Critical phenomena and the Kondo problem". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 47, 773. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.47.773](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.47.773)
Kondo (1964). "Resistance Minimum in Dilute Magnetic Alloys". *Prog. Theor. Phys.* 32, 37. [doi:10.1143/PTP.32.37](https://doi.org/10.1143/PTP.32.37)

name: Flat-band stiffness bounds T_BKT in moiré superconductors
summary: A 2D superconductor orders by BKT, so its $T_c$ is bounded by the superfluid stiffness. In magic-angle graphene's flat bands the conventional stiffness, proportional to bandwidth, is tiny, and a quantum-geometric term set by the band's quantum metric (bounded below by its Chern number) is proposed to supply it; recent kinetic-inductance measurements report stiffness consistent with that term.
map: k_BT_{\rm BKT}=\frac{\pi}{2}D_s(T_{\rm BKT}^-),\quad D_s=D_s^{\rm conv}+D_s^{\rm geom},\ D_s^{\rm geom}\propto\int g_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf k)\,d^2k
sources: Cao et al. (2018). "Unconventional superconductivity in magic-angle graphene superlattices". *Nature* 556, 43. [arXiv:1803.02342](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02342)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Mermin–Wagner and BKT physics in atomically thin crystals
summary: Two-dimensional superconductors (ion-gated MoS₂, few-layer NbSe₂, oxide interfaces) are analysed as vortex-unbinding transitions, using $V\propto I^3$ at $T_{\rm BKT}$ and the universal stiffness jump. In van der Waals magnets, easy-plane anisotropy gives 2D-XY behaviour, while Ising anisotropy (monolayer CrI₃) allows true long-range order despite Mermin–Wagner.
map: V\propto I^{a(T)},\ a(T_{\rm BKT})=3;\quad \rho_s(T_{\rm BKT}^-)=\tfrac{2}{\pi}k_BT_{\rm BKT}
sources: Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Two meanings of 'topological' order
summary: Both go beyond Landau's local order parameter. The BKT transition is the unbinding of vortices, defects classified by $\pi_1(S^1)=\mathbb Z$; topological order instead labels gapped $T=0$ phases by ground-state degeneracy and anyons. In both, proliferating point excitations destroy the ordered phase: free vortices above $T_{\rm BKT}$, and thermally excited anyons in a 2D toric code at any $T>0$.
breaks: The BKT phase is gapless with quasi-long-range order and has neither topological degeneracy nor long-range entanglement. Topological order is a gapped quantum phase that in 2D does not survive any nonzero temperature. 'Topological' refers to real-space defects in one case and to global ground-state structure in the other.
sources: Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)
Wen (1990). "Topological orders in rigid states". *Int. J. Mod. Phys. B* 4, 239. [doi:10.1142/S0217979290000139](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0217979290000139)

name: First law in a comoving volume gives the fluid equation
summary: Applying dU=−p dV adiabatically to a comoving volume gives the cosmological continuity equation, so each component's equation of state w=p/ρ fixes ρ∝a^{-3(1+w)}. A cosmological constant (w=−1) keeps its density fixed as the volume grows; its negative pressure balances the energy books.

name: Virial thermostat: stars heat up as they lose energy
summary: For a star in hydrostatic equilibrium the virial theorem gives total energy E=−K, so radiating energy away makes it contract and heat up (Kelvin–Helmholtz contraction). The same negative heat capacity keeps nuclear burning self-regulating: excess energy expands and cools the core.

name: Saha equation and cosmic recombination
summary: Chemical equilibrium μ_p+μ_e=μ_H between ideal gases gives the Saha equation. Photons outnumber baryons by 1/η≈1.6×10⁹, so hydrogen only recombines near k_BT≈0.3 eV, far below the 13.6 eV binding energy, and this sets the last-scattering surface.

name: Metastable and coexisting phases as dark-matter detectors
summary: Bubble chambers such as PICO keep a fluorocarbon superheated, as a metastable liquid. A nuclear recoil that deposits enough energy inside the critical radius nucleates a bubble (Seitz theory), and the threshold is tuned so electron recoils do not. Dual-phase xenon TPCs run at liquid–vapour coexistence so that drifted electrons are pulled into the gas, where they produce the S2 signal.

name: Clausius–Clapeyron runaway greenhouse sets the HZ inner edge
summary: Water-vapour pressure rises exponentially with temperature, so warming adds more greenhouse gas. Once the atmosphere is mostly steam, outgoing thermal radiation saturates near 280 W m⁻² (the Simpson–Nakajima limit) and the oceans evaporate. This defines the inner edge of the habitable zone.
sources: Kasting, Whitmire & Reynolds (1993). "Habitable Zones around Main Sequence Stars". *Icarus* 101, 108. [doi:10.1006/icar.1993.1010](https://doi.org/10.1006/icar.1993.1010)

name: Condensation curves and equilibrium chemistry in exoplanets
summary: Clouds form where a species' partial pressure meets its Clausius–Clapeyron saturation curve along the atmosphere's pressure–temperature profile: silicate and iron clouds on hot giants, KCl and Na₂S on cooler ones. Baseline compositions come from minimizing the Gibbs free energy. JWST spectra are read as departures from that baseline caused by vertical quenching and photochemistry.

name: White-dwarf crystallization and phase separation
summary: The core of a cooling white dwarf is a Coulomb plasma that freezes when the coupling Γ reaches about 175. Latent heat, plus oxygen sinking as the carbon–oxygen mixture phase-separates (a binary-mixture phase diagram), slows the cooling. Gaia sees this as a pile-up in the white-dwarf cooling sequence.

name: Adiabatic gradient, Γ₁ and stellar stability
summary: Stellar stability criteria are thermodynamic response functions. Convection starts when the radiative gradient exceeds ∇_ad (Schwarzschild criterion), and partial ionization lowers both ∇_ad and Γ₁. A star is dynamically unstable if its pressure-weighted Γ₁ drops below 4/3, and helioseismology measures Γ₁ inside the Sun to test the equation of state.

name: Γ₁<4/3 instabilities: core collapse and pair instability
summary: Some processes absorb energy without raising the pressure: iron photodisintegration and electron capture in collapsing cores, and electron–positron pair creation in very massive oxygen cores. They push Γ₁ below 4/3 and trigger collapse. Pair instability produces (pulsational) pair-instability supernovae and a predicted black-hole mass gap.
sources: Woosley, Heger & Weaver (2002). "The evolution and explosion of massive stars". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 74, 1015. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.74.1015](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.74.1015)

name: Friends-of-friends halos and cosmic-web percolation
summary: The friends-of-friends halo finder links particles closer than b≈0.2 times the mean separation, so its halos are continuum-percolation clusters. Percolation statistics of over- and underdense regions were also an early quantitative test of the cosmic web's connected, filamentary topology.

name: Reionization as percolation of ionized bubbles
summary: Ionized regions around early galaxies grow and merge until they form a spanning cluster. Simulations and upcoming 21-cm maps are interpreted by treating this overlap phase as a percolation transition, using cluster-size and topology statistics.

name: Degenerate-matter equation of state for compact stars
summary: Counting states of indistinguishable fermions in the grand-canonical ensemble gives a pressure that survives at T=0; this equation of state, with Sommerfeld finite-temperature and ionic heat-capacity corrections, sets white-dwarf structure and cooling ages.

name: 21-cm spin temperature as a two-level Boltzmann ratio
summary: The populations of hydrogen's two hyperfine levels define a spin temperature through the Boltzmann factor. T_s is a weighted mean of the CMB, gas-kinetic and Lyman-α colour temperatures (Wouthuysen–Field coupling). The 21-cm signal appears in absorption when T_s is below T_CMB and in emission when it is above.

name: Negative heat capacity and gravothermal catastrophe in clusters
summary: The virial theorem gives self-gravitating systems a negative heat capacity, which the canonical ensemble cannot represent (ensembles become inequivalent). A core that loses heat to its halo contracts and gets hotter, so isothermal spheres are unstable once the centre-to-edge density ratio exceeds 709. Globular clusters therefore undergo core collapse, which binary heating halts.

name: Entropic/emergent gravity as a MOND-like alternative
summary: Verlinde proposed that gravity is an entropic force arising from information on holographic screens. He later proposed that de Sitter entropy adds an 'apparent dark matter' force that scales like MOND, with a₀~cH₀. The idea is speculative and contested.
breaks: It has no accepted derivation from microphysics, and key steps assume Newton's law. Its galaxy-scale predictions are under strain from dwarf-galaxy, cluster and Solar System tests.

name: Lynden-Bell violent relaxation as maximum-entropy statistics
summary: Lynden-Bell maximized the coarse-grained entropy of a collisionless system whose fine-grained phase-space density is conserved. That incompressibility acts like an exclusion principle and gives a Fermi–Dirac-like distribution. It explains why rapid collapse gives every star the same velocity dispersion regardless of mass.
breaks: Relaxation stops before it is complete as the potential settles. The predicted equilibria have infinite mass, and simulated (NFW-like) halos do not follow Lynden-Bell's distribution.

name: CMB as a Bose–Einstein photon gas
summary: The CMB is the most precisely measured Planck spectrum (FIRAS, T0=2.7255 K). Expansion redshifts frequency and temperature together, so the Bose–Einstein form survives. Late energy release would leave a chemical-potential (μ) distortion, now bounded at |μ|<9×10⁻⁵.
sources: Mather et al. (1994). "Measurement of the cosmic microwave background spectrum by the COBE FIRAS instrument". *Astrophys. J.* 420, 439. [doi:10.1086/173574](https://doi.org/10.1086/173574)

name: Thermal history: g_*, entropy conservation, relic neutrinos
summary: In the radiation era the universe is a quantum ideal gas of relativistic species. Energy and entropy densities count boson degrees of freedom, with fermions weighted by 7/8, and comoving entropy is conserved. Electron–positron annihilation heats photons but not the already decoupled neutrinos, giving T_ν/T_γ=(4/11)^{1/3} and N_eff≈3.044.
sources: Planck Collaboration (2020). "Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters". *Astron. Astrophys.* 641, A6. [arXiv:1807.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209)

name: Fuzzy dark matter as a degenerate Bose field
summary: Ultralight bosons (m~10⁻²² eV) have such large occupation numbers that they behave as a classical wave obeying the Schrödinger–Poisson equations. Their kiloparsec de Broglie wavelengths form solitonic, condensate-like cores, and gravitational relaxation can condense Bose stars. Claims that all axion dark matter forms one coherent BEC are disputed.
sources: Hui, Ostriker, Tremaine & Witten (2017). "Ultralight scalars as cosmological dark matter". *Phys. Rev. D* 95, 043541. [arXiv:1610.08297](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.08297)

name: Fermi degeneracy pressure and the Chandrasekhar limit
summary: Electron degeneracy pressure P∝n^{5/3} softens to P∝n^{4/3} once electrons are relativistic. An n=3 polytrope then has a single allowed mass, the Chandrasekhar limit. The same Fermi-gas physics for neutrons, plus nuclear forces, sets the maximum mass of neutron stars.
sources: Chandrasekhar (1931). "The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs". *Astrophys. J.* 74, 81. [doi:10.1086/143324](https://doi.org/10.1086/143324)
Oppenheimer & Volkoff (1939). "On Massive Neutron Cores". *Phys. Rev.* 55, 374. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.55.374](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.55.374)

name: Degenerate cores and the helium flash
summary: In low-mass red giants the helium core is electron-degenerate, so its pressure barely depends on temperature. When helium ignites, the core heats without expanding, which defeats the virial thermostat, and the runaway helium flash continues until degeneracy is lifted. At the other extreme, blackbody radiation pressure dominates in massive stars.

name: Adhesion model: Zel'dovich flow as Burgers/KPZ
summary: Adding a small viscosity to the Zel'dovich approximation gives the Burgers equation for the comoving velocity, which a Cole–Hopf transform linearizes. Written for the velocity potential it is the noiseless KPZ equation, and its shocks reproduce the sheets, filaments and nodes of the cosmic web.
map:

breaks: The viscosity is artificial. Matter sticks inside shocks, so there is no shell crossing or virialization within halos, and the randomness comes from initial conditions rather than from KPZ's noise.
sources: Kardar, Parisi & Zhang (1986). "Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 56, 889. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889)

name: Solar flares as self-organized-criticality avalanches
summary: Flare energies follow a power law across many decades. Lu and Hamilton modelled the coronal magnetic field as a slowly driven sandpile whose reconnection avalanches reproduce that distribution, which made flares a leading astrophysical example of self-organized criticality.
breaks: Waiting-time statistics show memory and clustering that simple SOC does not predict, and the power-law index varies. A power law alone does not prove criticality, and the underlying physics is MHD reconnection.

name: Boltzmann hierarchy, Silk damping, non-equilibrium recombination
summary: CMB anisotropies come from solving the linearized photon Boltzmann equation with a Thomson collision term (the multipole hierarchy in CAMB/CLASS). The photons' finite mean free path lets the photon–baryon fluid diffuse, which erases the small-scale peaks (Silk damping). Peebles' rate equation shows that recombination lags behind Saha equilibrium.

name: SIDM halos as a conducting gas, then gravothermal collapse
summary: With σ/m~1 cm² g⁻¹, dark-matter self-scattering conducts heat like a dilute gas. It first builds an isothermal core, which addresses the cusp–core problem. Because the core has negative heat capacity, it can then undergo gravothermal collapse as globular clusters do, a process now invoked for unusually dense subhalos.
sources: Tulin & Yu (2018). "Dark matter self-interactions and small scale structure". *Phys. Rep.* 730, 1. [arXiv:1705.02358](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.02358)

name: Thermal freeze-out sets the relic annihilation cross-section
summary: Integrating the Boltzmann equation over momenta gives a rate equation for the dark-matter number density. Annihilations freeze out once n⟨σv⟩ falls below H, at m/T≈20–25. Matching the observed Ω_DM fixes the 'thermal' ⟨σv⟩≈3×10⁻²⁶ cm³ s⁻¹ that gamma-ray searches in dwarf galaxies aim to test.
map: \dot n+3Hn=-\langle\sigma v\rangle(n^2-n_{\rm eq}^2),\ \Omega h^2\approx\frac{3\times10^{-27}\,{\rm cm^3\,s^{-1}}}{\langle\sigma v\rangle}

name: Collisionless Boltzmann and Jeans equations for the Galaxy
summary: Two-body relaxation times are far longer than the Galaxy's age, so stars obey the collisionless Boltzmann (Vlasov) equation. Its velocity moments, the Jeans equations, turn Gaia kinematics into a measurement of the local dark-matter density. The Gaia phase spiral is a collisionless system caught partway through phase mixing.
map: \partial_tf+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla f-\nabla\Phi\cdot\partial_{\mathbf v}f=0,\ t_{\rm relax}\approx\frac{N}{8\ln N}t_{\rm cross}
breaks: There is no collision term and so no H-theorem: the system relaxes by phase mixing and violent relaxation, not toward a Maxwellian.

name: Neutrino trapping and diffusion in core collapse
summary: Above about 10¹² g cm⁻³ the neutrino mean free path (∝E_ν⁻²) is far smaller than the core, so neutrinos are trapped. They leak out by diffusion from a neutrinosphere over about 10 s, with nearly Fermi–Dirac spectra. Supernova simulations solve the Boltzmann transport equation for them, and the ~13 s neutrino burst from SN 1987A confirmed the timescale.

name: Gamow peak: Maxwellian tail times tunnelling
summary: A thermonuclear rate is the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution multiplied by the Coulomb-tunnelling probability. The product peaks at the Gamow energy, about 6 keV for the pp reaction in the solar core where k_BT≈1.35 keV. The resulting steep temperature dependence, for example a ⁸B neutrino flux ∝T_c^{~24}, makes solar neutrinos a sensitive thermometer of the core.

name: Stochastic inflation: inflaton Langevin dynamics
summary: Averaged over a Hubble patch, the inflaton gets a random kick of size H/2π per e-fold from modes crossing the horizon. It therefore obeys a Langevin equation, and its probability distribution a Fokker–Planck equation. This underlies eternal inflation and the first-passage (stochastic-δN) predictions of non-Gaussian tails that matter for primordial black holes.

name: Excursion sets: halo mass function as first passage
summary: Smoothing the linear density field on ever smaller scales makes δ perform a random walk in the variance S=σ²(M). The halo mass function is the distribution of first crossings of the collapse barrier δ_c≈1.686, which reproduces Press–Schechter including its ad hoc factor of 2.
breaks: The walk is Markovian only for a sharp-k filter. Realistic filters and ellipsoidal collapse need non-Markovian corrections and moving barriers.

name: Kompaneets equation and the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect
summary: Repeated Compton scattering off Maxwellian electrons makes photons diffuse in frequency according to a Fokker–Planck equation, the Kompaneets equation. Its n² stimulated-emission term makes the steady state a Bose–Einstein distribution. In hot cluster gas it shifts CMB photons to higher frequency, producing the thermal SZ y-distortion used to find clusters.

name: Diffusive shock acceleration as a random walk with escape
summary: Charged particles scattered by magnetic turbulence random-walk back and forth across a shock. Each crossing cycle gives a fixed fractional energy gain, and each cycle carries a fixed probability of escaping downstream. The competition produces a power law, E⁻² for a strong shock; energy-dependent diffusion through the Galaxy then steepens it to the observed ~E⁻²·⁷.
sources: Fermi (1949). "On the Origin of the Cosmic Radiation". *Phys. Rev.* 75, 1169. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.75.1169](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.75.1169)
Bell (1978). "The acceleration of cosmic rays in shock fronts – I". *Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc.* 182, 147. [doi:10.1093/mnras/182.2.147](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/182.2.147)

name: Dust coagulation: Smoluchowski kinetics and Brownian growth
summary: Grain growth in protoplanetary disks is modelled with the Smoluchowski coagulation equation. Collision kernels come from Brownian motion for small grains and from turbulence and drift for larger ones. Gas drag in the Epstein (kinetic) regime sets the stopping time and Stokes number, which control settling, radial drift and the bouncing and fragmentation barriers.

name: Fokker–Planck stellar dynamics: relaxation, friction, evaporation
summary: Chandrasekhar treated the cumulative effect of weak stellar encounters as Brownian motion: a Fokker–Planck equation with a drag term (dynamical friction) and a velocity-diffusion term. In star clusters this drives mass segregation and the evaporation of stars scattered above the escape speed, about 0.7% of a Maxwellian per relaxation time.

name: Radiative diffusion as a photon random walk
summary: Inside a star a photon travels only up to about a centimetre before it is scattered or absorbed, so energy moves by diffusion. Fick's law with a Rosseland-mean opacity gives the radiative temperature gradient. Escaping the solar core takes 10⁴–10⁵ yr, compared with R/c≈2 s for a straight path.

name: Stochastically excited p-modes as noise-driven oscillators
summary: Solar acoustic modes are damped and also driven by random forcing from convection near the surface. Each behaves like a Langevin oscillator whose power spectrum is a Lorentzian with a linewidth set by the damping rate. This model is the basis of mode fitting in helioseismology and in asteroseismology of solar-like stars.
sources: Christensen-Dalsgaard (2002). "Helioseismology". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 74, 1073. [arXiv:astro-ph/0207403](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0207403)

name: Kibble–Zurek defect formation and the monopole problem
summary: When a symmetry breaks, causally disconnected regions pick independent vacua, leaving at least one defect per correlation volume; Zurek fixed the frozen correlation length using critical exponents. GUT monopoles made this way would overclose the universe, a key motivation for inflation. The scaling has been tested in superfluid helium, liquid crystals and cold atoms.
sources: Linde (1982). "A new inflationary universe scenario: A possible solution of the horizon, flatness, homogeneity, isotropy and primordial monopole problems". *Phys. Lett. B* 108, 389. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(82)91219-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(82)91219-9)

name: Old inflation as a supercooled first-order transition
summary: Guth's inflation began as supercooling of a GUT phase transition. A Landau-type finite-temperature potential with a metastable false vacuum drives exponential expansion, which bubble nucleation was meant to end. The bubbles never percolate, so 'new' slow-roll inflation replaced the scenario.
sources: Guth (1981). "Inflationary universe: A possible solution to the horizon and flatness problems". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 347. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.347](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.347)

Linde (1982). "A new inflationary universe scenario: A possible solution of the horizon, flatness, homogeneity, isotropy and primordial monopole problems". *Phys. Lett. B* 108, 389. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(82)91219-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(82)91219-9)

name: Effective field theory of large-scale structure
summary: Integrating out the non-linear short-scale modes leaves an effective fluid. Its stress tensor has cutoff-dependent coefficients, such as the sound speed c_s², fixed by matching, exactly as in Wilsonian renormalization. Renormalized and time-RG perturbation theories resum loops to push predictions to mildly non-linear scales.

name: Fusion power plant as heat engine
summary: A fusion reactor's net electricity is bounded by thermal-cycle (Rankine/Carnot) efficiency of the blanket coolant loop, while the plasma energy balance uses Lawson-type gain analogous to engine power balance.

name: Plasma phase transitions and crystals
summary: Dusty-plasma crystals, Wigner crystallization and the plasma phase transition in dense hydrogen are phase-coexistence problems treated with chemical potential and equation-of-state constructions.

name: Magnetic pressure and MHD thermodynamics
summary: Ideal MHD closes with adiabatic equation of state and magnetic pressure; plasma beta compares thermal and magnetic pressure, and interchange stability uses entropy-like invariants pV^γ.

name: Percolation and insulator–metal transitions
summary: Pressure ionization and metallization in dense matter are sometimes modelled with percolation of conducting regions or bound-state clusters.
breaks: Real metallization is a quantum many-body phenomenon, not purely geometric.

name: Percolation of plasmoids and field lines
summary: Field-line connectivity and merging plasmoid chains in reconnection layers have been described with percolation concepts, including Rechester–Rosenbluth-like stochastic field-line transport thresholds.
breaks: Dynamics and MHD constraints, not static random geometry, control the plasmoid hierarchy.

name: Equations of state for warm dense matter
summary: HED equations of state are built from free-energy models and ensemble methods (Saha ionization equilibrium, path-integral Monte Carlo, DFT-MD) applied to partially ionized, degenerate matter.
